statement: A lift starts on floor 5. It makes 3 moves. Each move takes it up 1 floor or down 1 floor. On how many different floors could it finish?

choices.misconception: I listed the floors 2, 4, 6 and 8 and also counted floor 5, where it started.
I counted floors 2 to 8 but left out floor 5, without checking which floors can really be reached.
I counted every floor from 2 to 8.
I counted the different ways the lift can move, not the floors where it can finish.

hints: Draw a tree: after each move, write the floor.
A tree diagram shows every way the moves can go. Different paths can end on the same floor, so list the end floors and count each floor only once.
After 1 move it is on 4 or 6. After 2 moves it is on 3, 5 or 7. Do one more move from each.

solutions.reliable: Use a tree. After 1 move: 4 or 6. After 2 moves: 3, 5 or 7. After 3 moves: 2, 4, 6 or 8. There are 8 paths, but they finish on only 4 different floors: 2, 4, 6 and 8. The idea to keep: a tree counts paths, and then you check how many different endings those paths share.
solutions.elegant: Three moves of 1 floor change the floor by an odd number, and 5 plus an odd number is even. The lift is also at most 3 floors away from 5. The even floors from 2 to 8 are 2, 4, 6 and 8, so 4 floors.

whyOnTest: Counting end points instead of paths shows whether a solver can read a tree diagram, not just draw one.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
